captions: Hello, and welcome to Camday English, Stage 8. In this lesson: Should homework be banned?
Read a balanced discursive essay and identify points for and against.
Here are some new words. Discursive. Discussing different sides of a question. Balanced.
Giving equal attention to different views. Counter-argument. An argument against another argument.
And some more words. Evidence. Facts or information that support an idea. Stance.
A person's opinion or position on something. Evaluate. Judge how good or important something is.
Time for a question. The video will stop. Which word means: discussing different sides of a question?
Now some grammar: Passive reporting structures. Use it is said, thought or believed that, or X is said to,
to report general opinions without saying who holds them.
For example: It is believed that homework improves results. For example: Homework is thought to cause stress.
Now listen, and read along. Should homework be banned?
Homework has been part of school life for generations, but many people now question whether it is useful.
This essay will consider both sides.
Supporters of homework argue that it helps students practise skills and remember what they have learned.
It is also thought to develop independence and good study habits, which students will need later in life.
On the other hand, it is often argued that too much homework causes stress and leaves little time for sleep,
exercise and family.
Some studies suggest that, for younger students, homework has only a small effect on results.
Furthermore, not all students have a quiet place to work at home, which may be unfair.
In conclusion, banning homework completely may not be the answer. However, it seems sensible to set shorter,
more meaningful tasks, so that students can learn without losing their free time.
Another question. The video will stop. What will the essay do?
Well done! Today you learned new words, like discursive, balanced, counter-argument.
You practised passive reporting structures. And you read Should homework be banned?
Now try the practice questions. See you next time!

captions: Hello, and welcome to Camday English, Stage 8. In this lesson: Opening the debate.
Use hedging language and formal phrases to present a view politely in a debate.
Here are some new words. Motion. The statement that is discussed in a debate. Proposition.
The team that supports the motion. Opposition. The team that is against the motion.
And some more words. Rebuttal. An answer that shows an argument is wrong. Hedge.
Make a statement less strong or certain. Concede. Admit that something is true.
Time for a question. The video will stop. Which word means: the statement that is discussed in a debate?
Now some grammar: Hedging and polite disagreement. Use hedging, such as may, might, it could be argued,
tends to and perhaps, and polite phrases, such as I see your point, but, or with respect,
to sound reasonable. For example: Social media may increase anxiety.
For example: I see your point, but the evidence suggests otherwise.
Now listen, and read along. Opening speech for the opposition.
Madam Chair, members of the proposition, ladies and gentlemen.
The motion today is: ‘This house would ban mobile phones in schools.’ We, the opposition,
believe that a complete ban would be a mistake. I concede that phones can be a distraction.
It is true that some students tend to check messages in lessons.
However, a ban is perhaps too extreme a solution. Firstly, phones can be powerful learning tools.
Students use them to look up words, record experiments and access on lai lessons.
Secondly, many parents want their children to be able to contact them,
especially on the journey to and from school. My opponents may argue that rules are hard to enforce.
With respect, I would suggest that clear rules – phones away in lessons,
allowed at break – could solve the problem without a ban. For these reasons, I urge you to oppose the motion.
Another question. The video will stop. What is the motion?
Well done! Today you learned new words, like motion, proposition, opposition.
You practised hedging and polite disagreement. And you read Opening speech for the opposition.
Now try the practice questions. See you next time!

B.ctx:
Should homework be banned?
Homework has been part of school life for generations, but many people now question whether it is useful. This essay will consider both sides.
Supporters of homework argue that it helps students practise skills and remember what they have learned. It is also thought to develop independence and good study habits, which students will need later in life.
On the other hand, it is often argued that too much homework causes stress and leaves little time for sleep, exercise and family. Some studies suggest that, for younger students, homework has only a small effect on results. Furthermore, not all students have a quiet place to work at home, which may be unfair.
In conclusion, banning homework completely may not be the answer. However, it seems sensible to set shorter, more meaningful tasks, so that students can learn without losing their free time.
